title: Nemotron-CC-Math: High-Quality Math Pretraining at Scale
one_liner: Building better math datasets from the messy web requires careful extraction and cleanup to preserve mathematical notation.
lead: Training AI models on math requires clean datasets. But getting math off the internet is hard—web pages mangle equations, mix them with garbage, and lose structure. This paper fixes that by carefully extracting math from the web and cleaning it up, unlocking more math training data than ever before.

problem.h2: The web has math, but broken math
paras: The internet is full of math content: textbooks, lecture notes, research papers, homework solutions. To train a model that solves math problems, we want to use all of it. But there is a problem: web pages store math in many different ways. Some use MathJax (a library that renders math in browsers), others use KaTeX, others raw LaTeX markup, others MathML (yet another standard). When you download a page as plain text, all these formats get mangled. Symbols turn into garbage. Equation structure breaks apart.

A naive approach would be to find any page with an equation and dump the text. That fails badly: the page has navigation menus, ads, comments, warnings—all that noise gets mixed in with the math. The equations themselves get corrupted. A research paper's careful equation becomes scrambled text. You end up with a huge dataset where half the math is wrong.

callout.html: Render the page in a browser-like way first, so all equation formats become visible. Then clean up the text intelligently, standardize equations to LaTeX, and remove the noise.

steps.text: Use lynx to display equations in text form, converting MathJax/KaTeX to visible symbols.
Break the rendered page into text blocks, each likely to be one idea or one equation.
Keep only chunks that contain equations or code; discard navigation and ads.
Use a language model to remove boilerplate, fix corruption, and standardize notation.
Convert all equations to LaTeX, a standard mathematical notation format.

paras: The paper changes the extraction pipeline—the code that turns a webpage into training data. Instead of naive text-dump, it adds rendering and intelligent cleanup.

hidden.name: structural fidelity
paras: Structural fidelity measures how well an extracted equation keeps its original meaning and format. A perfectly fidelity extraction looks like the original; a corrupt extraction has missing pieces or scrambled symbols.
The paper estimates this by checking: Do the equations render? Are all symbols present? Is the logical flow intact? They count how many equations pass each check.

heat.caption: Darker means higher structural fidelity. Highlighted steps actively boost it.

reads.html: Structural fidelity is how well the extracted math stays true to the original—symbols present, equations unbroken, meaning clear.
The paper preserves math by recovering it across multiple formats and standardizing to LaTeX, measurable by whether extracted equations remain valid and complete.

paras: The problem is that equations live in HTML in many formats. A naive text dump does not understand that these formats exist, so it copies raw markup. Lynx is a text-mode browser—it actually renders the page like a browser does, turning all those format differences into plain text equations. That removes the first barrier to understanding.

The second problem is noise. A page is not just math; it has menus, ads, author names, dates. If you keep all of it, the training data is mostly garbage. The pipeline splits the page into chunks and filters to only chunks containing equations or code. That makes the data denser in signal.

The third problem is inconsistency. Even after extraction, the math is in different notations. Some use different symbol names; some use different spacing; some are partially broken from rendering. An LLM is good at recognizing corrupted math and repairing it while preserving meaning. It also standardizes everything to LaTeX, so the training data is uniform.

stages.s: raw web pages in multiple formats
render via lynx to convert all equation types to text
split into chunks and filter for math
use LLM to fix corruption and standardize

math.words: For each equation e in the extracted dataset, the quality score is one if e is complete and consistent, zero if corrupted. The dataset quality is the fraction of equations that pass both checks.
symbols: equations that render without error and keep all original symbols
all equations in the extracted dataset
the fraction of extraction that succeeds

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Naive dump produces 60 intact equations (60% fidelity) because some turn to garbage.
Render + cleanup: lynx recovers 20 more, LLM fixes 10 corrupted ones. Now 90 intact (90% fidelity).
Result: 30 percentage-point improvement by preserving structure, not losing work.

math.note: Fidelity is simple: the fraction of math that survives extraction unchanged. Higher fidelity means less training time wasted on broken examples.

charts.title: Naive extraction
charts.note: Without rendering and cleanup, most extracted equations are mangled or mixed with garbage.

charts.title: This paper (render + LLM clean)
charts.note: Rendering all equation types and intelligent cleanup preserves mathematical structure and removes boilerplate.

items.html: Some pages use custom equation syntax. Lynx cannot render every dialect. Pages with rare formats fall back to text dump, losing equations.
The language model might invent symbols or change meaning while fixing corruption. A guessed symbol is as bad as a missing one.
The noise filter discards chunks that look like boilerplate but contain equations. A strict filter loses signal.

items.b: Done right: verification and human review.
items.html: Sample the output and check that extracted equations match the originals. Use conservative filtering. Verify LLM repairs with a second model before trusting them.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Download five web pages with math. Extract equations using the naive approach and the paper's approach. For each page, count how many extracted equations still render correctly and match the original meaning. The paper's pipeline should extract more valid equations with fewer corruptions than the naive approach. Show side-by-side before-and-after for one equation to make the improvement concrete.
demo.closing: The demo must show that rendering and cleanup recover equations that naive extraction loses, turning web text into valid math data.
